newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian traders see LME nickel falling, zinc rising.
newsitem.headline: Asian traders see LME nickel falling, zinc rising.

text.p: Nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are set for a further decline after workers at Canada's Inco Ltd's Sudbury plant accepted a deal to end a strike over the weekend, Asian metal traders said on Monday.
But the zinc outlook remains on an upward trend, they said.
"We've seen quite a lot of stop-loss selling after it (three-month nickel) breached the $7,000 level. It could fall further towards $6,400," a trader at a European firm said.
"Zinc's likely to move higher as we can't really see the next resistance. We haven't seen much selling by producers."
By 0240 GMT, the benchmark three-month was quoted at $6,810/60 per tonne, down from $6,850 at 1815 GMT on Friday and the kerb's close at $6,970.
On Saturday, union representatives said that striking Inco Ltd workers in Sudbury voted 80 percent in favour of accepting the latest labour deal from the giant nickel miner to end a four-week strike.
In early Asia, zinc stood at $1,433/38, compared with $1,433 at 1815 GMT on Friday and the kerb's close at $1,428.

Traders in Tokyo said rumours that Swiss trader Glencore had requested the LME to check the quality of Chinese zinc, known as "Torch", were helping zinc continue its bull run. Zinc reached a new 6-3/4 year high in London on Friday.
No official comment was immediately available from Glencore, the LME or Chinese authorities.

Traders expected copper to move back towards $2,500 in nervous trade ahead of the option declaration on Wednesday, while aluminium is set to remain in the recent trading range in the absence of fresh factors.

Asian metal traders remained cautious of any moves related to South Korea. An LG Metals spokesman said on Thursday the company had sold 10,000 tonnes of copper to Metallgesellschaft AG and that the cargo would be shipped to Singapore.
